card.chief_complaint: left facial droop and slurred speech

ask.changes_what: Positive: fingerstick now, treat, and observe for recurrence (sulfonylurea/renal failure -> admit); negative: keep glucose check but move to cardiac/neurologic causes of the spell.
ask.contraindications: None; the history must never delay a point-of-care glucose in any patient with altered mental status, syncope or focal deficit.
ask.do_not_use_when: Never rely on symptom history alone in an obtunded, post-ictal or focally weak patient - measure glucose immediately.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypoglycemia with sulfonylurea, insulin overdose, renal failure or alcohol needs monitored admission and repeated glucose; persistent deficit after glucose correction is a stroke workup.
ask.how: Ask specifically about insulin or sulfonylurea use (drug, dose, timing of last dose), missed or delayed meals, alcohol, recent renal or hepatic decline, and prodromal autonomic symptoms (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger) or neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, drowsiness, difficulty speaking, weakness). Confirm with a fingerstick glucose at the time of symptoms.
ask.negative_finding: No exposure to insulin or secretagogues and no critical illness, cortisol/hormone deficiency or alcohol makes drug-induced hypoglycemia unlikely, but a measured glucose is still required because neuroglycopenia can present without warning symptoms.
ask.pitfalls: Long-standing diabetes and beta-blockers blunt autonomic warning symptoms so neuroglycopenic presentation (confusion, focal deficit) may be the only clue; sulfonylurea hypoglycemia recurs for 24-72 h so a single corrected glucose is not the end of the episode.
ask.positive_finding: Insulin/secretagogue exposure plus a missed meal, alcohol or renal impairment and autonomic or neuroglycopenic prodrome makes hypoglycemia likely; Whipple's triad (symptoms, documented low glucose, resolution with glucose) confirms it.
ask.prerequisites: A collateral history when the patient is confused; the medication list including recently added sulfonylureas, insulin dose changes, or drugs that potentiate them.
ask.title: Hypoglycemia history: insulin/sulfonylurea use, missed meals, adrenergic or neuroglycopenic symptoms

ask.changes_what: Positive: give thiamine before glucose, start symptom-triggered benzodiazepines, check glucose/ammonia. Negative: pursue other AMS causes; still consider Wernicke if malnourished.
ask.contraindications: CIWA-Ar is unreliable in patients who cannot communicate (intubated, delirious from another cause, severe dementia).
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use CIWA-Ar to drive sedation in patients who cannot communicate or whose agitation may be from another cause (sepsis, hypoxia, head injury, hypoglycemia).
ask.escalation_warning: Seizure, fever, marked autonomic instability or hallucinations with confusion 48-96 h after the last drink suggest delirium tremens or Wernicke; give IV thiamine and escalate care.

evidence.citation: Aertgeerts B, Buntinx F, Kester A. The value of the CAGE in screening for alcohol abuse and alcohol dependence in general clinical populations: a diagnostic meta-analysis. J Clin Epidemiol. 2004;57(1):30-39.
evidence.population: Hospital inpatients from studies pooled in a diagnostic meta-analysis (10 studies overall)
evidence.quote: the pooled sensitivity is far better in inpatients (0.87) than in primary care patients (0.71) or ambulatory patients (0.60)
evidence.reference_standard: DSM criteria for alcohol abuse/dependence (structured interview)
evidence.target_condition: DSM-defined alcohol abuse or dependence; CAGE score >=2 (inpatients)

evidence.citation: Aertgeerts B, Buntinx F, Kester A. The value of the CAGE in screening for alcohol abuse and alcohol dependence in general clinical populations: a diagnostic meta-analysis. J Clin Epidemiol. 2004;57(1):30-39.
evidence.population: Primary care patients from pooled studies
evidence.quote: the pooled sensitivity is far better in inpatients (0.87) than in primary care patients (0.71) or ambulatory patients (0.60)
evidence.target_condition: DSM-defined alcohol abuse or dependence; CAGE score >=2 (primary care)

evidence.citation: Aertgeerts B, Buntinx F, Kester A. The value of the CAGE in screening for alcohol abuse and alcohol dependence in general clinical populations: a diagnostic meta-analysis. J Clin Epidemiol. 2004;57(1):30-39.
evidence.population: General clinical populations, 10 pooled studies (inpatient, primary care, ambulatory)
evidence.quote: The likelihood ratios seem to be relatively constant over the populations (overall LR+:3.44;LR-:0.18)
evidence.target_condition: DSM-defined alcohol abuse or dependence; CAGE score >=2 (all populations)

ask.how: Ask the four CAGE questions (Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener), quantity/frequency, and the exact time of the last drink. Score CIWA-Ar items at the bedside: nausea, tremor (arms extended), sweats, anxiety, agitation, tactile/auditory/visual disturbances, headache, orientation (0-67).
ask.negative_finding: CAGE <2 lowers but does not exclude an alcohol use disorder (pooled LR- 0.18; sensitivity only 0.60 in ambulatory patients). A drink within the last few hours makes withdrawal an unlikely cause of current symptoms.
ask.pitfalls: CAGE detects abuse/dependence, not hazardous drinking, and performs poorly in women, prenatal and primary-care populations. CIWA-Ar is a severity scale, not a diagnostic test, and is inflated by pain, sepsis, hypoglycemia and anxiety.
ask.positive_finding: CAGE >=2 raises the probability of DSM alcohol abuse/dependence (pooled LR+ 3.44; sensitivity 0.87 in inpatients). Last drink 6-24 h ago with tremor/sweats/agitation fits early withdrawal; 48-96 h fits delirium tremens.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to answer or a collateral historian; CIWA-Ar requires a communicative patient.
ask.title: Alcohol use (CAGE) and time since last drink; tremor, diaphoresis, agitation (CIWA items)

examine.changes_what: Positive: treat as stroke until imaged, especially if anticoagulated (urgent CT for hemorrhage). Negative in a dizzy patient: still needs HINTS/gait assessment; does not exclude stroke.
examine.contraindications: None. Do not stand a patient who is vomiting, severely ataxic or hypotensive to test gait.
examine.do_not_use_when: Never use a normal three-item screen to exclude stroke in acute vertigo, ataxia, diplopia or visual loss; posterior-circulation strokes frequently have none of the three findings.
examine.escalation_warning: New focal deficit in an anticoagulated patient is intracranial hemorrhage until proven otherwise: urgent CT and reversal pathway. Any focal deficit within the reperfusion window is time-critical.

evidence.citation: Goldstein LB, Simel DL. Is this patient having a stroke? JAMA. 2005;293(19):2391-2402.
evidence.population: Pooled studies of patients with neurologically relevant symptoms, modern neuroimaging (RCE systematic review)
evidence.quote: acute facial paresis, arm drift, or abnormal speech increases the likelihood of stroke (LR of > or =1 finding = 5.5; 95% CI, 3.3-9.1)
evidence.reference_standard: Final diagnosis after neuroimaging and laboratory tests

evidence.citation: Diagnostic accuracy of the physical examination in emergency department patients with acute vertigo or dizziness: a systematic review and meta-analysis for GRACE-3. Acad Emerg Med. 2023;30(5):552-578.
evidence.population: ED patients with acute vertigo or dizziness; 5 studies, 869 patients
evidence.quote: general neurologic examination-five studies, 869 patients, pooled sensitivity 46.8% (95% confidence interval [CI] 32.3%-61.9%, moderate certainty) and specificity 92.8% (95% CI 75.7%-98.1%
evidence.target_condition: Central cause (stroke, hemorrhage, other) of acute vertigo/dizziness - general neurologic examination abnormal

evidence.citation: Diagnostic accuracy of the physical examination in emergency department patients with acute vertigo or dizziness: a systematic review and meta-analysis for GRACE-3. Acad Emerg Med. 2023;30(5):552-578.
evidence.population: ED patients with acute vertigo or dizziness; 4 studies, 893 patients
evidence.quote: limb weakness/hemiparesis-four studies, 893 patients, sensitivity 11.4% (95% CI 5.1%-23.6%, high) and specificity 98.5% (95% CI 97.1%-99.2%, high)
evidence.target_condition: Central cause of acute vertigo/dizziness - limb weakness/hemiparesis

evidence.citation: Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome: three-step bedside oculomotor examination more sensitive than early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging. Stroke. 2009;40(11):3504-3510.
evidence.location: Table 1 (PAVS n=25 vs CAVS n=76), Stroke 2009;40:3504 (PMC4593511)
evidence.population: 101 consecutive high-risk AVS patients (25 peripheral, 76 central) at a stroke referral center
evidence.reference_standard: MRI (or CT) for stroke; normal MRI plus clinical follow-up for peripheral
evidence.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome (stroke or other central lesion) - any general neurologic sign including truncal ataxia

examine.how: Brief structured screen: facial symmetry on smile, pronator drift with arms held out and eyes closed for 10 s, and speech (repeat a sentence, name objects). Add gaze (ask to look left/right), visual fields by confrontation, finger-nose and heel-shin, and gait if safe, because dizzy or confused patients often lack the three classic items.
examine.negative_finding: A normal focal screen lowers stroke probability modestly overall (LR about 0.4 for absence of face/arm/speech findings) but is insensitive for posterior-circulation stroke: pooled sensitivity of the general neurologic exam in acute vertigo is under 50%, and in Kattah's AVS cohort general signs were absent in 49% of central lesions.
examine.pitfalls: Confusion, aphasia and encephalopathy from hypoglycemia, seizure or intoxication mimic focal deficits; a normal screen in a dizzy patient is falsely reassuring, so add HINTS and a gait test. Old deficits must be compared with baseline.
examine.positive_finding: Any new focal finding (facial paresis, arm drift, dysarthria/aphasia, gaze palsy, hemisensory loss, limb ataxia) strongly favours a central lesion; in dizzy patients such general neurologic signs are highly specific for a central cause (pooled specificity about 93%; limb weakness 98.5%).
examine.prerequisites: Bedside glucose; note baseline deficits, time last known well and anticoagulant use. Patient must be able to follow at least one-step commands or the screen defaults to observation of asymmetry.
examine.title: Focal deficit screen: facial droop, arm drift, speech (Cincinnati/NIHSS-lite)

examine.changes_what: Positive: activate stroke pathway/immediate imaging and time-critical reperfusion assessment. Negative: lowers probability but still image if dizziness, ataxia or visual symptoms.
examine.contraindications: None; if the patient cannot cooperate, observe spontaneous facial symmetry and limb movement instead.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a negative screen to exclude posterior-circulation stroke in a patient with acute dizziness, ataxia, diplopia or visual field loss; use HINTS/gait assessment and imaging pathways instead.
examine.escalation_warning: Any positive item with symptom onset within the reperfusion window is a time-critical emergency; do not delay activation for a glucose result unless hypoglycemia is confirmed and deficits resolve with correction.

evidence.citation: Goldstein LB, Simel DL. Is this patient having a stroke? JAMA. 2005;293(19):2391-2402.
evidence.population: Pooled studies of patients with suspected stroke evaluated with modern neuroimaging (RCE systematic review)
evidence.quote: LR of > or =1 finding = 5.5; 95% CI, 3.3-9.1 ... LR of 0 findings = 0.39; 95% CI, 0.25-0.61
evidence.reference_standard: Final diagnosis after neuroimaging and relevant laboratory tests
evidence.target_condition: Acute stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic) among patients with neurologically relevant symptoms

evidence.citation: Kothari RU, Pancioli A, Liu T, Brott T, Broderick J. Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale: reproducibility and validity. Ann Emerg Med. 1999;33(4):373-378.
evidence.population: Convenience sample of 171 ED and neurology inpatients, 49 with stroke/TIA
evidence.quote: abnormality in any 1 of the 3 stroke scale items had a sensitivity of 66% and specificity of 87% in identifying a stroke patient.
evidence.reference_standard: Discharge diagnosis of stroke or TIA
evidence.target_condition: Stroke or TIA (any 1 of 3 CPSS items abnormal, scored by physician)

evidence.citation: Kothari RU, Pancioli A, Liu T, Brott T, Broderick J. Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale: reproducibility and validity. Ann Emerg Med. 1999;33(4):373-378.
evidence.population: Same 171-patient convenience sample; subgroup with anterior circulation stroke
evidence.quote: The sensitivity was 88% for identification of patients with anterior circulation strokes.
evidence.reference_standard: Discharge diagnosis of stroke, anterior circulation
evidence.target_condition: Anterior circulation stroke (any 1 of 3 CPSS items abnormal)

examine.how: Ask the patient to smile or show teeth and look for asymmetric facial movement; have them close eyes and hold both arms out palms-up for 10 seconds, watching for one arm drifting down; ask them to repeat a simple sentence and listen for slurring, wrong words, or inability to speak. Any one abnormal item is a positive screen.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of all three findings lowers but does not exclude stroke (LR about 0.4); posterior-circulation strokes, which often present with dizziness or ataxia, are commonly missed by this screen (Kothari: 66% sensitivity overall vs 88% for anterior circulation).
examine.pitfalls: Bell palsy, old deficits, intoxication, hypoglycemia and seizure mimics all produce false positives; isolated vertigo, ataxia, visual field loss and neglect are not captured, so a negative screen must not stop a stroke work-up in a dizzy patient.
examine.positive_finding: Any new facial paresis, arm drift, or abnormal speech; in patients with neurologically relevant symptoms this raises the probability of stroke (pooled LR about 5.5).
examine.prerequisites: Patient awake enough to follow simple commands; check a fingerstick glucose alongside the screen. Note time last known well.
examine.title: Facial droop, arm drift, abnormal speech (Cincinnati/FAST screen)

examine.changes_what: Forehead spared: stroke pathway/imaging. Forehead involved and isolated: Bell palsy work-up and early steroids; any additional neurological sign redirects to central causes.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use forehead involvement alone to exclude stroke in patients with vascular risk factors, vertigo, diplopia, ataxia, limb or gaze findings, or bilateral/recurrent palsy.
examine.escalation_warning: Any additional neurological deficit, sudden onset with headache, or forehead-sparing pattern warrants urgent stroke assessment.
examine.how: Ask the patient to raise the eyebrows, close the eyes tightly against resistance, show the teeth and puff the cheeks; compare sides. Forehead and eye closure preserved with lower-face weakness = upper motor neuron (central) pattern; forehead, eye closure and lower face all weak on one side = lower motor neuron (peripheral) pattern. Also check ear canal, other cranial nerves and limbs.
examine.negative_finding: Involvement of the forehead and eye closure indicates a peripheral (facial nerve) lesion, consistent with Bell palsy when isolated and rapid in onset; it does not exclude a pontine stroke (nucleus/fascicle lesion gives a peripheral pattern), Ramsay Hunt, Lyme disease, otitis or tumour.
examine.pitfalls: Bilateral cortical innervation of the forehead makes sparing incomplete in some central lesions, and mild peripheral palsies can look forehead-sparing early. Pontine infarcts and facial-nucleus lesions produce a 'peripheral' pattern with a central cause; look for crossed signs, gaze palsy or other cranial nerve deficits.
examine.positive_finding: Forehead sparing with lower facial weakness indicates a central (supranuclear) lesion and should be treated as a possible stroke until proven otherwise; accompanying limb weakness, dysarthria, gaze palsy or diplopia strongly favours stroke.
examine.prerequisites: Adequate cooperation; note pre-existing asymmetry, ptosis or previous palsy.
examine.title: Forehead sparing (central) vs forehead involvement (peripheral) in facial weakness

examine.changes_what: Present: treat as high-risk for dissection and obtain CT angiography of the aorta urgently; absent: does not change dissection probability.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of deficit to exclude dissection; do not give thrombolysis for stroke with chest/back pain until the aorta is imaged.
examine.escalation_warning: Any new focal deficit with chest/back pain, pulse deficit, or hypotension is a surgical emergency; activate CT angiography and vascular/cardiothoracic surgery immediately.

evidence.citation: Ohle R, Kareemi HK, Wells G, Perry JJ. Clinical Examination for Acute Aortic Dissection: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2018.
evidence.population: ED patients evaluated for suspected acute aortic dissection; 3 pooled studies (I2 0%); dissection prevalence across the 9 review studies ranged 21.9%-76.1%
evidence.quote: neurologic deficit (n = 3, specificity = 95%, positive likelihood ratio [LR+] = 4.4, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 3.3-5.7, I2 = 0%)
evidence.reference_standard: Advanced imaging (CT/MR/TEE), surgery or autopsy per included study
evidence.target_condition: Acute aortic dissection — finding PRESENT = neurologic deficit

evidence.citation: Klompas M. Does this patient have an acute thoracic aortic dissection? JAMA. 2002.
evidence.population: Pooled from 21 studies of >=18 consecutive patients with confirmed thoracic aortic dissection (1966-2000)
evidence.reference_standard: Confirmed thoracic aortic dissection (imaging, surgery or autopsy)
evidence.target_condition: Acute thoracic aortic dissection — finding PRESENT = focal neurological deficit (sensitivity only; case series of confirmed dissection)

examine.how: In any patient with acute chest, back or abdominal pain, perform a brief screening neurologic exam: speech, facial symmetry, pronator drift and grip in both arms, leg strength, sensation, and pupils (Horner). Note any deficit that is new, fluctuating, or accompanied by pain, and check bilateral arm blood pressures and pulses at the same time.
examine.negative_finding: Most dissections have no neurologic deficit (pooled sensitivity ~17%), so its absence does not lower the probability meaningfully.
examine.pitfalls: Deficits may be transient (syncope, paraparesis from spinal ischemia) or missed if pain dominates; stroke without pain is far more often primary cerebrovascular disease. Painless dissection presenting as stroke occurs and is a thrombolysis hazard.
examine.positive_finding: A focal neurologic deficit in a patient with acute chest or back pain raises the probability of aortic dissection (pooled LR+ 4.4, specificity 95%), and the combination of stroke syndrome with pain should prompt aortic imaging before thrombolysis.
examine.prerequisites: Patient able to cooperate; compare with baseline function.
examine.title: Focal neurologic deficit (limb weakness, aphasia, Horner) accompanying chest/back pain
